subtype: Approach: pairs the list of things to avoid with a positive target [Revision]
passage: I'm Rehana, and I share a flat with Pallavi, so I watched her yearly plan take shape at the kitchen table. The first version was all rules: no takeaways, no late nights before work, no extra projects, no arguing with her manager. It looked tidy. On Sunday, though, she read it aloud, stopped, and said, 'This tells me what to avoid, not where I'm going.' She took a blank sheet, wrote the twelve months down the side, and beside each one put a single aim: finish the first module of her design course in February, present at the team demo in March, and so on. The rules went at the bottom of the page in small writing. I can't tell what she felt, but she pinned it above her desk and looked at it every morning.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi put the rules on the new sheet?
qa.a: Pallavi put the rules at the bottom of the page in small writing.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been thinking when she stopped reading aloud?
qa.a: Pallavi may have realised that the plan was only about avoiding things and felt a little disappointed, though Rehana can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do if she misses a monthly aim?
qa.a: Pallavi could move the aim to the next month and ask what got in the way, since the aims should guide the year and not become a source of guilt.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen the change in the plan?
qa.a: Rehana probably noticed the plan going from tidy to purposeful, though Rehana can't say how Pallavi felt.

grounding: Shows a person noticing that a plan is only defensive and adding one clear aim per month, so avoidance rules serve a direction.

subtype: Approach: pairs the list of things to avoid with a positive target [Revision]
passage:
First week of January. Yamini, a new team lead at the Kochi design studio, wrote her plan for the year: no missed deadlines, no client complaints, no burnt-out designers, no scope creep. She showed it to Gargi, her senior.
Gargi read it twice. "These are all things you don't want. What do you want?"
Yamini had no answer that day.
Mid-February. The team hit every deadline and had zero complaints. But they were bored, and two designers asked to switch teams. Yamini opened the plan again and saw it clearly. Every line was a wall. None of them was a road.
March. She rewrote the plan. The avoid list stayed, but above it she added one aim per month. March: launch a portfolio page. April: each designer leads one client pitch. She pinned it on the board. The two designers stayed.

qa.q: What did Yamini's team aim to do in April?
qa.a: Each designer leads one client pitch.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when Gargi asked what she wanted?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little caught out, since she had no answer that day.

qa.q: What else could Yamini add to keep the new aims working, and why?
qa.a: She could review each month's aim with the team at the month's end, so the direction stays shared and not just pinned on a board.

qa.q: How might the two designers see the new plan?
qa.a: They may feel there is now something to grow toward, not just rules to follow, which is why they chose to stay.

grounding: It shows a team lead noticing her plan is only defensive and adding one clear aim per month so the rules to avoid serve a direction.

subtype: Approach: pairs the list of things to avoid with a positive target [Revision]
passage:
Chinmay, you're saying your whole plan is just a list of don'ts. Let your Reena Masi tell you something.
When I was twenty-five and running my first clinic shift roster, I wrote rules for myself. No double shifts. No gaps at night. No nurse working three weekends running. It was a good list. Nobody could complain.
But after two months I felt like a traffic policewoman. Just stopping bad things. My roster was safe and my nurses were tired of it and so was I.
One evening I thought, where am I actually trying to go? So I added one aim each month. First month, every nurse gets one full weekend off. Next month, each senior teaches one junior a skill on shift.
Same don'ts, but now they were guarding something. That's what changed, beta.

qa.q: What was Reena's aim for the first month?
qa.a: Every nurse gets one full weekend off.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling after two months of only following her rules?
qa.a: Reena felt tired and flat, like a traffic policewoman just stopping bad things.

qa.q: When Reena felt like a traffic policewoman, what else could she have done, and how might it have gone?
qa.a: She could have kept only the don'ts, but the nurses would likely have stayed tired and the roster would have had no purpose.

qa.q: How might the nurses have seen the new monthly aims?
qa.a: They may have felt more cared for and more motivated, with full weekends off and chances to learn skills from seniors.

grounding: It shows a woman noticing her roster plan is only defensive and adding one positive aim each month so her avoidance rules serve a direction.
